archetype.name: Rebuilding (rookie QB handoff)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff that has rebuilt a league-worst offense into a functional one, but whose defense still can't get off the field, and which has now turned the ball over to a rookie quarterback.

report.headline: Real offensive progress, a defense that stops nothing, and now a rookie QB.
report.take:
Start with where this came from. Last year's Raiders went 3-14 with the league's worst offense (offensive EPA ranked 32nd, 14.2 points a game). Under first-year coach Klint Kubiak, with Kirk Cousins starting the first nine games, the offense climbed to the middle of the league (offensive EPA 16th) and the scoreboard looks better still: 26.4 points a game, 8th. That climb is real but flattered. The yardage is middling (332.7 a game, 15th), and the scoring has been helped by a defense that takes the ball away (14 takeaways, 4th) and special teams that rank 7th in EPA. The engine was Cousins and a pass offense that kept him clean: a 3.2% sack rate, 2nd in the league, and 300-yard games against Kansas City, Buffalo and the Rams.

The defense is the problem, and it is not a new one. Its pass rush is one of the league's best (a 27.2% pressure rate, 3rd), yet it ranks 31st in success rate allowed, dead last against short passes, 28th in red-zone touchdown rate and 26th on third down. That profile is a group that hurries quarterbacks and still loses the down: quick throws beat the rush and runs get through for chunks (explosive run rate allowed 31st). The result is the most points allowed in football, 29.8 a game. KC, the Rams and San Francisco each ran for 189 yards or more. Outside of a strong 2023, this franchise's defense has sat in the bottom third almost every year in the history block.

The 3-0 start hid all of this. Those wins came against Miami, the Chargers and New Orleans, offenses that rank 25th, 32nd and 22nd today, and the defense forced turnovers in bunches in all three games. Once the schedule turned to real offenses, the defense got exposed and the only win since was a 38-33 shootout with the Jets. The record itself is about fair: the point differential (-38) implies 3.4 wins against the actual four, and they're 50% in one-score games. The Book has underrated them all year (a 66.7% cover rate, 5th), mostly because the offense kept losing games close.

Now the floor has moved. Fernando Mendoza started Week 10 (the dossier doesn't say why Cousins didn't) and took six sacks with -8 passing EPA in a 21-13 loss to Seattle. The run game is the worst in football by almost every line measure, so a rookie gets no help from it, and Brock Bowers, the top target, is day-to-day with an ankle. The question for the rest of the year is not the playoffs. It is whether Mendoza can stabilize behind a line that protected a veteran well but can't move anyone in the run game.

strengths.title: Elite pressure from the front
strengths.body: The defense gets home: a 27.2% pressure rate ranks 3rd and the QB-hit rate 8th. The sack total (19, 16th) lags the pressure, so some of that should turn into more sacks. The catch is that pressure alone hasn't stopped offenses that throw quick, so it is a weapon that needs coverage to support it.

strengths.title: A pass offense rebuilt from the bottom
strengths.body: After a league-worst offense in 2025, the passing game ranks 14th in EPA per play and the line allowed sacks on just 3.2% of dropbacks, 2nd. That was a veteran quarterback getting the ball out on time behind a line that holds up in pass protection. The protection should mostly carry over, but the efficiency was Cousins-era and Mendoza's first start already looked very different.

strengths.title: Hidden yards: takeaways and teams
strengths.body: Fourteen takeaways (4th) and the 7th-best special teams EPA have handed the offense short fields and padded a scoring rank (8th) that sits well above its yardage rank. Takeaways come in streaks and many arrived in the opening three weeks, so expect this to give back some of its value.

concerns.title: A defense that can't win downs
concerns.body: The defense ranks 31st in success rate allowed, 32nd against short passes and 28th in red-zone touchdown rate, which is how a top-three pass rush coexists with the most points allowed in the league. Offenses are getting the ball out before the pressure lands and running through the second level. The franchise's defensive history says this isn't a one-year blip, and nothing in the schedule ahead suggests a fix.

concerns.title: The worst run game in football
concerns.body: Ashton Jeanty has the carries, but the line gives him nothing: 1.39 yards before contact and a 32.2% run success rate, both last in the league, with 3.01 yards a carry. That is a blocking problem first, and it leaves the offense one-dimensional. With a rookie now at quarterback it becomes the biggest structural issue on the roster.

concerns.title: The quarterback change reset everything
concerns.body: Mendoza's first start produced 143 passing yards, -8 passing EPA and six sacks against a line that had allowed the second-lowest sack rate in the league with Cousins. Some of that is a rookie holding the ball. A league-best pass rush also loomed for him, and Bowers left that game hurt. Expect growing pains, not a repeat of the first nine weeks.

trend.note: A 3-0 start against weak offenses gave way to a losing run once the schedule stiffened. The defense got shredded in October, five turnovers sank the San Francisco game, and the offense managed 17 and 13 points in the last two with the quarterback change landing in Week 10.

nextGame.headline: A rookie quarterback on the road against Denver's pass rush
nextGame.body:
Denver is 7-2 but plays like a .500 team: a +1.3 point differential per game (15th), net EPA 15th, and the most wins over expected in the league thanks to a perfect record in one-score games. Its offense is thin (279.2 yards a game, 30th; success rate 27th), which is why the total sits at 40.5. The 10-point spread is less about Denver's dominance than about the Raiders' quarterback. The Broncos' strength is the side that matters here: a pass defense 10th in EPA, 5th against deep throws, 2nd in QB-hit rate and 3rd in sacks. That is the worst kind of opponent for a rookie who just took six sacks. Their weakness is the run defense (26th in rush EPA allowed, 31st in missed-tackle rate), but the Raiders have the league's least productive run game to aim at it.

Availability tilts both ways. Bowers is questionable with an ankle that Kubiak called "not as bad as we thought, but still a significant injury"; if he sits, Michael Mayer (49 targets) becomes the middle-of-the-field option. Kwity Paye is questionable and Thomas Booker is out, which thins a front that is the defense's one real asset. Denver's secondary is in worse shape: both starting safeties, Talanoa Hufanga and Brandon Jones, are out, corner Riley Moss is questionable with a concussion and Kris Abrams-Draine is out. On offense, Jaylen Waddle is questionable with a concussion.

waysToWin.title: Attack the middle without Denver's safeties
waysToWin.body: Denver already allows 0.44 EPA per target to tight ends (28th), and it will play without two safeties who each logged 90%+ of snaps. Quick throws to Bowers or Mayer and Jeanty out of the backfield also beat the pass rush, the rookie's best way through this game.

waysToWin.title: Keep it low and close
waysToWin.body: Denver's offense rarely creates easy yards. If the Raiders' pass rush can get to Bo Nix and the takeaways return, this becomes a field-position game. A team that is perfect in one-score games is due to lose one sooner or later.

waysToWin.title: Make Denver tackle Jeanty
waysToWin.body: Denver misses tackles at the second-highest rate in the league and ranks 26th in rush EPA allowed. Even with no push up front, Jeanty breaking first contact could keep the offense on schedule and off Denver's pass rush.

waysToLose.title: The pass rush swallows the rookie
waysToLose.body: Denver ranks 2nd in QB-hit rate with 26 sacks. Mendoza took six sacks in his first start, and this is a road game against a better rush. Drives that die on second-and-long are a short path to a two-score deficit.

waysToLose.title: Short passes march Denver downfield
waysToLose.body: Denver leans pass (6th in pass rate over expected), and the Raiders are the league's worst defense against short throws. Even a limited offense can string together long drives against a unit that ranks 32nd in success rate allowed.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers on the road
waysToLose.body: Denver ranks 5th in takeaways. A rookie forced into obvious passing downs with no run game behind him is exactly the setup that produced the five-turnover loss at San Francisco.

nextGame.watch: Mendoza's time to throw on early downs: if the Raiders get the ball out fast to Bowers, Mayer and Jeanty against a Denver secondary missing both starting safeties, they can hang. If he holds it, Denver's rush ends this early.

restOfSeason.body:
The Cousins-era offense isn't what you should project from here. Expect a passing game that takes more sacks and scores less while Mendoza learns, with no run game to lean on. The defense's pressure is real and should keep producing sacks, but the coverage and tackling problems behind it have held up across ten games and most of this franchise's recent history, so points allowed should stay near the bottom of the league. Takeaways and special teams, which propped up the scoring rank, are the most likely things to cool.

The schedule offers a split. Two dates with Denver and a trip to Kansas City are hard, and Cleveland's defense ranks 9th. Home games with the Chargers and Titans (both 1-8) and a trip to Arizona (31st in defensive EPA) are where the wins are. Realistically this is a 6-8 win team whose real stakes are Mendoza's development and finding a run game for next year.

confidence.note: Ten games of data, but the offense's profile was built by a different quarterback than the one now starting.
